source_text: ZELARE quod bonum videas et invidere melioribus leve apud quosdam et modicum crimen videtur, fratres dilectissimi; dumque existimatur leve esse et modicum, non timetur; dum non timetur, contemnitur; dum contemnitur, non facile vitatur, et fit caeca et occulta pernicies: quae, dum minus perspicitur ut caveri a providentibus possit, improvidas mentes latenter affligit. Porro autem Dominus prudentes esse nos jussit, et cauta sollicitudine vigilare praecepit, ne adversarius vigilans semper et semper insidians, ubi in pectus obrepserit, de scintillis conflet incendia, de parvis maxima exaggeret, et, dum remissis et incautis leniore aura et flatu molliore blanditur, procellis ac turbinibus excitatis, ruinas fidei et salutis ac vitae naufragia moliatur. Excubandum est itaque, fratres dilectissimi, atque omnibus viribus elaborandum ut inimico saevienti et jacula sua in omnes corporis partes quibus percuti et vulnerari possumus, dirigenti sollicita et plena vigilantia repugnemus, secundum quod Petrus apostolus in Epistola sua praemonet et docet dicens: Sobrii estote et vigilate, quia adversarius vester diabolus tamquam leo rugiens circuit, aliquem devorare quaerens. Circuit ille nos singulos, et tamquam hostis clausos obsidens, muros explorat, et tentat an sit pars aliqua murorum minus stabilis et minus fida, cujus aditu ad interiora penetretur. Offert oculis formas illices et faciles voluptates, ut visu destruat castitatem. Aures per canora musica tentat, ut soni dulcioris auditu solvat et molliat christianum vigorem. Linguam convicio provocat, manum injuriis lacessentibus ad petulantiam caedis instigat; ut fraudatorem faciat, lucra opponit injusta; ut animam pecunia capiat, ingerit perniciosa compendia; honores terrenos promittit, ut coelestes adimat; ostentat falsa, ut vera subripiat: et cum latenter non potest fallere, exerte atque aperte minatur, terrorem turbidae persecutionis intentans, ad debellandos Dei servos inquietus semper et semper infestus, in pace subdolus, in persecutione violentus. Quamobrem, fratres dilectissimi, contra omnes diaboli fallaces insidias vel apertas minas stare debet instructus animus et armatus, tam paratus semper ad repugnandum quam est ad impugnandum semper paratus inimicus. Et, quoniam frequentiora sunt tela ejus quae latenter obrepunt, magisque occulta et clandestina jaculatio quo minus perspicitur, hoc et gravius et crebrius in vulnera nostra grassatur, ad haec quoque intelligenda et depellenda vigilemus ex quibus est zeli et livoris malum. Quod si quis penitus inspiciat, inveniet nihil magis Christiano cavendum, nihil cautius providendum quam ne quis invidia et livore capiatur; ne quis fallentis inimici caecis laqueis implicatus, dum zelo frater in fratris odia convertitur, gladio suo nescius ipse perimatur. Quod ut colligere plenius et manifestius perspicere possimus, ad caput ejus atque originem recurramus. Videamus unde zelus, et quando et quomodo coeperit. Facilius enim a nobis malum tam perniciosum vitabitur, si ejusdem mali et origo et magnitudo noscatur. Hinc diabolus inter initia statim mundi et periit primus et perdidit. Ille angelica majestate subnixus, ille Deo acceptus et charus, postquam hominem ad imaginem Dei factum conspexit, in zelum malivolo livore prorupit, non prius alterum dejiciens instinctu zeli quam ipse zelo ante dejectus, captivus antequam capiens, perditus antequam perdens, dum, stimulante livore, homini gratiam datae immortalitatis eripit, ipse quoque id quod prius fuerat amisit. Quale malum est, fratres dilectissimi, quo angelus cecidit, quo circumveniri et subverti alta illa et praeclara sublimitas potuit, quo deceptus est ipse qui decepit! Exinde invidia grassatur in terris, dum livore periturus magistro perditionis obsequitur, dum diabolum qui zelat imitatur, sicut scriptum est: Invidia autem diaboli mors introivit in orbem terrarum. Imitantur ergo illum qui sunt ex parte ejus.
pass_a_gloss: To be zealous for what is good and to envy those who are better is considered a light and minor crime among some, most beloved brothers; and while it is considered light and minor, it is not feared; while it is not feared, it is despised; while it is despised, it is not easily avoided, and it becomes a hidden and secret destruction: which, while it is less perceived so that it can be avoided by the prudent, secretly afflicts the imprudent minds. Moreover, the Lord commanded us to be prudent and to be watchful with cautious solicitude, lest the adversary, always watching and always lying in wait, where he has crept into the breast, may kindle fires from sparks, may exaggerate great things from small ones, and, while he flatters the remiss and the incautious with a milder breeze and a softer breath, may threaten the shipwrecks of faith and salvation and life with excited storms and whirlwinds. Therefore, it is necessary to be watchful, most beloved brothers, and to strive with all our strength so that, with solicitous and full watchfulness, we may resist the savage enemy who directs his darts at all parts of the body by which we can be struck and wounded, according to what the apostle Peter warns and teaches in his Epistle, saying: Be sober and watch, because your adversary, the devil, like a roaring lion, goes around seeking someone to devour. He goes around each one of us, and like a hostile besieger, he explores the walls and tests whether there is any part of the walls that is less stable and less faithful, by which entrance he may penetrate to the interior. He offers to the eyes enticing forms and easy pleasures, so that he may destroy chastity by sight. He tempts the ears with melodious music, so that he may loosen and soften Christian vigor by the hearing of a sweeter sound. He provokes the tongue with abuse, he incites the hand to petulant murder with injuries that provoke; so that he may make a deceiver, he opposes unjust gains; so that he may capture the soul with money, he brings in destructive profits; he promises earthly honors, so that he may take away heavenly ones; he shows false things, so that he may steal away true ones: and when he cannot deceive secretly, he threatens openly and plainly, intending the terror of turbulent persecution, always restless and always hostile to the servants of God, cunning in peace, violent in persecution. Wherefore, most beloved brothers, the instructed and armed mind must stand against all the deceitful snares or open threats of the devil, as prepared always to resist as the enemy is always prepared to attack. And, since his darts which creep in secretly are more frequent, and the more occult and clandestine the darting is, the less it is perceived, and the more seriously and frequently it attacks our wounds, let us be watchful also to understand and repel these things, from which is the evil of jealousy and envy. But if anyone thoroughly examines, he will find that nothing is more to be avoided by a Christian, nothing more cautiously to be provided against, than that someone be taken by envy and envy; lest someone, caught in the blind snares of the deceiving enemy, while brotherly zeal is converted into hatred of a brother, unknowingly perish by his own sword. So that we may gather this more fully and perceive it more clearly, let us return to the head and origin of it. Let us see whence jealousy comes, and when and how it began. For this most pernicious evil will be more easily avoided by us if the origin and magnitude of the same evil are known. Hence the devil, among the beginnings of the world, perished first and was lost. He, supported by angelic majesty, he, accepted and dear to God, after he saw man made in the image of God, broke out into malicious jealousy and envy, not casting down another by the impulse of zeal before he himself was cast down by zeal, a captive before he took captive, lost before he caused loss, while, goaded by envy, he took away from man the gift of immortality, and he himself also lost what he had been before. What evil is this, most beloved brothers, by which an angel fell, by which that high and noble sublimity was able to be deceived and overthrown, by which he who deceived was himself deceived! From that time envy rages on earth, while the one who is about to perish by envy obeys the master of perdition, while he imitates the devil who envies, as it is written: But by the envy of the devil, death entered into the world. Therefore, those who are on his side imitate him.

pass_b_english: It seems like a light, minor offense to some of you, dear brothers, to be zealous for what is good and to envy those who are better. Because it is regarded as slight, no one fears it; because no one fears it, it is despised; and because it is despised, it is not easily avoided. It becomes a hidden, secret ruin that, precisely because it is barely noticed, escapes the prudent and secretly afflicts the careless. The Lord, however, commanded us to be prudent and to keep watch with careful concern, so that the adversary—always watching, always lying in wait—might not creep into our hearts and kindle fires from sparks, magnify great evils from small ones, and, while he flatters the lax and incautious with a gentle breeze and a softer breath, stir up storms and whirlwinds that threaten shipwreck of faith, salvation, and life. (1 Peter 5:8) Therefore, dear brothers, we must keep watch and strive with all our strength, so that with anxious, full vigilance we may resist the savage enemy who aims his darts at every part of the body by which we can be struck and wounded, just as the apostle Peter warns and teaches in his letter: 'Be sober and watch, because your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour.' He circles each one of us, and like a hostile besieger he probes the walls, testing whether any section is less stable or less trustworthy, so that through that breach he may penetrate to the interior. He offers enticing forms and easy pleasures to the eyes, to destroy chastity by sight. He tempts the ears with melodious music, so that the hearing of a sweeter sound may loosen and soften Christian vigor. He provokes the tongue with abuse; he incites the hand to violent murder through provoking injuries. To make a deceiver, he sets out unjust gains; to capture the soul with money, he brings in destructive shortcuts. He promises earthly honors, so that he may take away heavenly ones; he displays false things, so that he may steal the true. And when he cannot deceive secretly, he threatens openly and plainly, brandishing the terror of turbulent persecution—always restless, always hostile toward God's servants, cunning in peace, violent in persecution. Consequently, dear brothers, a mind that is instructed and armed must stand against all the devil's deceitful snares and open threats, as prepared to resist as the enemy is always prepared to attack. Since his darts that creep in secretly are more frequent, and the more hidden and clandestine the assault, the less it is perceived and the more seriously and often it ravages our wounds, we must also be watchful to recognize and repel these attacks, which spring from the evil of zeal and envy. If anyone examines the matter thoroughly, he will find nothing a Christian must avoid more carefully, nothing he must guard against more cautiously, than being seized by envy and malice—lest someone, caught in the blind snares of the deceiving enemy, while brotherly zeal turns into hatred of a brother, perish unknowingly by his own sword. So that we may grasp this more fully and see it more clearly, let us go back to its head and origin. Let us see where zeal comes from, and when and how it began. For we will avoid this most pernicious evil more easily if we know both its origin and its magnitude. From the very beginning of the world, the devil perished first and was lost. He, supported by angelic majesty, he, accepted and dear to God, after he saw man made in God's image, broke out into malicious zeal and envious malice. He did not cast down another by the impulse of zeal before he himself was cast down by zeal; he was a captive before he took captive, lost before he caused loss. Goaded by envy, he tore away from man the gift of immortality, and he himself lost what he had been before. What an evil this is, dear brothers, by which an angel fell, by which that high and noble sublimity could be deceived and overthrown, by which the deceiver himself was deceived! From that time envy has raged on earth, while the one doomed to perish by envy serves the master of perdition, while he imitates the devil who envies, as it is written: 'But by the envy of the devil, death entered the world.' Therefore those who belong to his party imitate him.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the Latin text. Pass A provides a faithful clause-by-clause rendering. Pass B is a fluent English version that maintains the theological nuances and causal relations. Scripture citations (1 Peter 5:8) are correctly identified and applied to the relevant text. The title 'Dangers of Jealousy and Envy' correctly names the thought of the passage.
